stem: What is meant by the **optimum temperature** of an enzyme?

options.content: The temperature at which the enzyme is denatured
options.rationale: At the optimum the enzyme works best; denaturation happens above it.

options.content: The temperature at which the enzyme works fastest
options.rationale: This is the definition.

options.content: The lowest temperature at which the enzyme works at all
options.rationale: Enzymes work slowly even at low temperatures; the optimum is where they work fastest.

options.content: 37 °C, for every enzyme
options.rationale: Each enzyme has its own optimum; many human enzymes are close to 37 °C, but not all enzymes.

explanation: The optimum temperature is the temperature at which an enzyme catalyses its reaction fastest. Below it the rate is lower because molecules move more slowly; above it the enzyme starts to be denatured.

stem: An enzyme from the human gut is kept at 5 °C for an hour and then warmed to 37 °C. What happens to its activity?

options.content: It stays at zero, because the cold denatured the enzyme.
options.rationale: Cold does not denature enzymes; only high temperature or extreme pH does.

options.content: It is highest at 5 °C and falls when the enzyme is warmed.
options.rationale: Human enzymes work fastest close to body temperature.

options.content: It is low at 5 °C and rises at 37 °C: cold does not denature it.
options.rationale: Low temperature makes enzymes inactive, not denatured.

options.content: The cold killed the enzyme, so it cannot work again when warm.
options.rationale: Enzymes are not alive, and cold does not damage their shape.

explanation: At 5 °C the molecules have little kinetic energy, so there are few collisions and the enzyme works very slowly. Its shape is not changed, so when it is warmed to 37 °C it works at full speed again.

stem: True or false: once an enzyme has been denatured by high temperature, cooling it down does not make it work again.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct. Denaturation is a permanent change in the shape of the active site.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true: denaturation is permanent, unlike the slowing caused by low temperature.

explanation: High temperature permanently changes the shape of an enzyme's active site, so the substrate no longer fits. Cooling the enzyme does not restore its shape, so it stays inactive.

stem: An enzyme works in the human stomach, where hydrochloric acid keeps the contents strongly acidic. Which is the most likely optimum pH of this enzyme?

options.content: pH 2
options.rationale: Enzymes are adapted to the conditions where they work, and the stomach is strongly acidic.

options.content: pH 7
options.rationale: pH 7 is neutral; the stomach is strongly acidic.

options.content: pH 8
options.rationale: pH 8 is slightly alkaline, like the small intestine.

options.content: pH 12
options.rationale: pH 12 is strongly alkaline.

explanation: Enzymes have an optimum pH that suits the place where they work. The stomach contents are strongly acidic (about pH 2), so a stomach enzyme such as pepsin works best at about pH 2.

stem: Complete the sentences about high temperatures.

payload.template: If the temperature rises far above the optimum, the shape of the enzyme's {{blank:site}} changes. The substrate can no longer fit, and the enzyme is said to be {{blank:word}}.

explanation: High temperatures change the shape of the active site, so the substrate no longer fits: the enzyme is denatured. Enzymes are not alive, so 'killed' is wrong.

stem: Why does food kept in a refrigerator go bad more slowly than food kept at room temperature?

options.content: Low temperature denatures all the enzymes in the food and in the microorganisms.
options.rationale: Cold does not denature enzymes; they work again when warmed.

options.content: The cold kills every microorganism living in the food.
options.rationale: Most microorganisms survive in a fridge; they just grow slowly.

options.content: The cold changes the pH of the food so that enzymes cannot work.
options.rationale: Cooling does not change the food's pH; it slows the enzymes.

options.content: Microbes' enzymes work slowly in the cold, so they decay food slowly.
options.rationale: Low temperature makes enzymes inactive, slowing decay.

explanation: At fridge temperatures enzymes have little kinetic energy and work very slowly, so decomposing bacteria and fungi grow and digest the food slowly. The enzymes are not denatured, which is why food decays quickly again once it is warmed.

stem:
The table shows the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction at different temperatures.

| Temperature / °C | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 | 60 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rate / arbitrary units | 6 | 13 | 25 | 38 | 17 | 0 |

Which description of the results is correct?

options.content: The rate increases steadily as the temperature increases.
options.rationale: The rate falls above 40 °C.

options.content: The rate is highest at 60 °C.
options.rationale: The rate at 60 °C is zero.

options.content: It rises from 10 °C to a peak at 40 °C, then falls steeply to zero at 60 °C.
options.rationale: It describes the rise, the peak and the steep fall, with values.

options.content: The rate falls from 10 °C to a low point at 40 °C and then rises again to 60 °C.
options.rationale: This is the reverse of the pattern.

explanation: The rate rises from 6 units at 10 °C to a peak of 38 units at 40 °C, then falls steeply to 17 units at 50 °C and to zero at 60 °C, where the enzyme is denatured.
hints: Find the highest rate first, then describe what happens on each side of it.

stem: In an amylase experiment, the starch took 75 s to disappear. Calculate the rate of reaction as $\dfrac{1000}{\text{time}}$. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
explanation: Rate $= \dfrac{1000}{75} = 13.333\ldots = 13.3$ to 1 decimal place.
hints: Divide 1000 by the time in seconds.

stem:
Sipho investigated the effect of temperature on the digestion of starch by amylase. He recorded the time taken for the starch to disappear at each temperature.

| Temperature / °C | Time for starch to disappear / s |
| --- | --- |
| 10 | 540 |
| 20 | 260 |
| 30 | 120 |
| 40 | 70 |
| 50 | 210 |
| 60 | Starch still present after 900 s |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the rate of reaction at 30 °C as $\dfrac{1000}{\text{time}}$. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: At which temperature was the rate fastest?

options.rationale: The longest time (540 s) means the slowest rate.
The time at 50 °C (210 s) is three times longer than at 40 °C.
The shortest time (70 s) means the fastest rate.
At 60 °C the starch was never digested.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Describe the effect of temperature on the time taken for the starch to disappear. Use data from the table.

points.description: From 10 °C to 40 °C the time decreases (from 540 s to 70 s)
Above 40 °C the time increases (210 s at 50 °C), and at 60 °C the starch is not digested at all

parts.explanation: As the temperature rose from 10 °C to 40 °C, the time fell from 540 s to 70 s. Above 40 °C the time rose again, to 210 s at 50 °C, and at 60 °C the starch was still present after 900 s.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why the starch was still present at 60 °C.

points.description: The amylase was denatured (by the high temperature)
The shape of the active site changed, so starch no longer fits / is not complementary / no enzyme-substrate complexes form

parts.explanation: At 60 °C the amylase was denatured: the shape of its active site changed, so starch molecules no longer fitted and could not be broken down.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: State how Sipho should keep the temperature of each tube constant during the test.

points.description: Use a thermostatically controlled water bath (or a water bath with a thermometer, adding hot or cold water as needed)

parts.explanation: Stand the tubes in a thermostatically controlled water bath set to the test temperature.

explanation: The rate at 30 °C is $\frac{1000}{120} = 8.3$. The shortest time, and so the fastest rate, was at 40 °C. Above the optimum the amylase is denatured, so at 60 °C the starch was never digested.
workedSolution:
1. (a) Rate $= \frac{1000}{120} = 8.33\ldots = 8.3$.
2. (b) The shortest time is 70 s, at 40 °C.
3. (c) Time falls from 540 s (10 °C) to 70 s (40 °C), then rises to 210 s (50 °C); no digestion at 60 °C.
4. (d) Amylase denatured: active site changed shape, starch no longer fits.
5. (e) A thermostatically controlled water bath.
hints: A shorter time means a faster rate.
What happens to the active site at high temperatures?

stem:
Nyasha investigated the effect of pH on catalase from potato. In each test she mixed potato extract with hydrogen peroxide solution and a buffer solution, and collected the oxygen in a gas syringe for 3 minutes.

| pH | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9 | 10 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Volume of oxygen in 3 minutes / cm³ | 3.0 | 10.5 | 19.5 | 27.0 | 22.5 | 12.0 | 4.5 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: State the optimum pH of this catalase, using these results.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the rate of oxygen production at pH 6, in cm³ per minute.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: State **two** variables, other than pH, that Nyasha should keep constant.

points.description: Temperature
Volume / concentration of hydrogen peroxide
Volume / concentration of potato extract (amount of enzyme)
Time over which oxygen is collected / volume of buffer

parts.explanation: Temperature (by using a water bath) and the volume and concentration of the hydrogen peroxide solution.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why very little oxygen was produced at pH 4.

points.description: pH 4 is far from the optimum, so the shape of the active site changes / the enzyme is (partly) denatured
Hydrogen peroxide no longer fits the active site, so few enzyme-substrate complexes form

parts.explanation: pH 4 is far from the optimum of pH 7. The acid changes the shape of catalase's active site, so hydrogen peroxide no longer fits and few enzyme-substrate complexes form.

explanation: The most oxygen (27.0 cm³) was collected at pH 7, so that is the optimum of the values tested. At pH 6 the rate is $19.5 \div 3 = 6.5$ cm³ per minute. Far from the optimum the active site changes shape, so the substrate no longer fits.
workedSolution:
1. (a) Largest volume: 27.0 cm³ at pH 7.
2. (b) Rate $= \frac{19.5\ \text{cm}^3}{3\ \text{min}} = 6.5\ \text{cm}^3/\text{min}$.
3. (c) For example, temperature and the volume of hydrogen peroxide.
4. (d) Active site changes shape away from the optimum pH; the substrate no longer fits.
hints: Rate = volume ÷ time.
Which part of the enzyme is affected by pH?

stem: An enzyme has an optimum temperature of 40 °C. Explain the effect of increasing the temperature from 10 °C to 60 °C on the rate of the reaction it catalyses. [5]

points.description: From 10 °C to 40 °C the rate increases
The molecules gain kinetic energy and move faster
More frequent (effective) collisions between enzyme and substrate / more enzyme-substrate complexes form per second
The rate is fastest at the optimum, 40 °C
Above 40 °C the enzyme is denatured: the bonds holding its shape break and the active site changes shape
The substrate no longer fits / is no longer complementary, so fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form and the rate falls (to zero by 60 °C)
Denaturation is permanent

answerSpec.modelAnswer: From 10 °C to 40 °C the rate increases. The enzyme and substrate molecules gain kinetic energy and move faster, so they collide more often: there are more effective collisions and more enzyme-substrate complexes form each second. The rate is fastest at the optimum, 40 °C. Above 40 °C the enzyme starts to be denatured: the bonds holding its shape break and the shape of the active site changes, so the substrate no longer fits. Fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form, and the rate falls steeply, reaching zero by 60 °C. This change is permanent.
answerSpec.markingNotes: Any five points; at least one mark must come from each side of the optimum for full marks.

explanation: Below the optimum, more kinetic energy means more effective collisions; above it, the active site changes shape and the enzyme is denatured.
hints: Explain the two sides of the optimum separately.

stem: Why does increasing the temperature from 20 °C to 30 °C increase the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction?

options.content: Molecules gain kinetic energy, collide more often and form more complexes.
options.rationale: More effective collisions each second means a faster rate.

options.content: The active site becomes larger, so more substrate molecules fit at once.
options.rationale: The active site does not grow; it keeps its shape until the enzyme starts to denature.

options.content: The enzyme starts to be denatured, which exposes more active sites.
options.rationale: Denaturation destroys the active site's shape and slows the reaction.

options.content: The heat supplies energy that the enzyme uses up in the reaction.
options.rationale: Enzymes are not used up, and the effect is on how fast molecules move.

explanation: At higher temperatures the molecules have more kinetic energy and move faster. They collide more often, so there are more effective collisions and more enzyme-substrate complexes form each second, giving a faster rate (up to the optimum).
hints: Think about how fast the molecules move.

stem: An enzyme with an optimum pH of 8 is added to a solution at pH 2. What is most likely to happen?

options.content: It works faster than at pH 8, because acid speeds up all reactions.
options.rationale: Moving away from the optimum pH slows an enzyme down.

options.content: It works very slowly or not at all: acid changes its active site.
options.rationale: pH 2 is far from its optimum, so the substrate no longer fits well.

options.content: Its optimum pH changes to 2 to match the solution.
options.rationale: An enzyme's optimum is fixed by its structure; it does not adjust.

options.content: It is unaffected, because pH changes only the substrate's shape.
options.rationale: pH changes the shape of the enzyme's active site.

explanation: At pH 2, six units away from its optimum, the enzyme's active site changes shape and it is likely to be denatured. The substrate no longer fits, so the enzyme works very slowly or not at all.
hints: How far is pH 2 from the optimum?

stem: True or false: every enzyme in the human body works fastest at pH 7.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Not true. Pepsin in the stomach works best at about pH 2, and trypsin in the small intestine at about pH 8.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct. Each enzyme has its own optimum pH, suited to where it works.

explanation: Enzymes have different optimum pH values that suit where they work: pepsin in the acidic stomach about pH 2, salivary amylase about pH 7 and trypsin in the small intestine about pH 8.
hints: Think about the enzyme that works in the stomach.

stem: To make maheu, a thin maize porridge is cooked, left to cool, and then a little malted (sprouted) sorghum or millet flour is stirred in. The malt contains amylase, which breaks starch down into sugars. Why is the porridge cooled **before** the malt is added?

options.content: Cooling stops the starch being broken down too quickly.
options.rationale: The aim is for the amylase to work; cooling to a warm temperature protects it.

options.content: Amylase works only below about 10 °C, like the enzymes in food in a fridge.
options.rationale: Amylase works faster in warm conditions, up to its optimum.

options.content: The heat would turn the malt into more starch.
options.rationale: Heat does not make starch from malt; it would denature the enzyme.

options.content: Hot porridge would denature the malt's amylase, so starch stays undigested.
options.rationale: The enzyme must be added below the temperature at which it is denatured.

explanation: Amylase is a protein. In hot porridge it would be denatured, its active site would change shape, and the starch would not be digested into sugars. Letting the porridge cool first keeps the enzyme active.
hints: What does a high temperature do to an enzyme?

stem:
Enzyme A comes from a human. Enzyme B comes from bacteria that live in a hot spring. The rates of their reactions were measured at different temperatures.

| Temperature / °C | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 | 60 | 70 | 80 | 90 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rate with enzyme A / arbitrary units | 10 | 21 | 35 | 14 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Rate with enzyme B / arbitrary units | 2 | 4 | 7 | 12 | 20 | 31 | 38 | 9 |

Which statement is supported by the data?

options.content: Both enzymes have the same optimum temperature.
options.rationale: A is fastest at 40 °C and B at 80 °C.

options.content: Enzyme B still works at 60 °C, but enzyme A has stopped.
options.rationale: At 60 °C, A gives a rate of 0 and B a rate of 20.

options.content: Enzyme B works faster than enzyme A at 30 °C.
options.rationale: At 30 °C, A gives 21 units and B only 4.

options.content: Enzyme A has an optimum temperature of about 80 °C.
options.rationale: Enzyme A stops working at 60 °C; its fastest rate is at 40 °C.

explanation: Enzyme A works fastest at 40 °C and is denatured by 60 °C. Enzyme B, from bacteria adapted to hot water, keeps its shape at high temperatures: it is still working at 60 °C and is fastest at 80 °C, before falling at 90 °C.
hints: Read across the table at 60 °C.
Find the highest rate in each row.

stem: The rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction was 25 units at 40 °C and 4 units at 55 °C. Calculate the percentage change in the rate. Show a decrease as a negative value.
explanation: Change $= 4 - 25 = -21$ units. Percentage change $= \dfrac{-21}{25} \times 100 = -84\%$.
hints: Divide the change by the starting value (the rate at 40 °C).

stem: Fresh pineapple contains a protease. A cook finds that a jelly made with gelatine, a protein, does not set when pieces of fresh pineapple are added, but it does set when tinned pineapple is used. Tinned pineapple is heated to a high temperature during canning. Which explanation is correct?

options.content: Heating makes tinned pineapple more acidic, which helps the jelly to set.
options.rationale: The difference is caused by the enzyme being denatured, not by acidity.

options.content: Fresh pineapple contains starch, which stops the gelatine from setting.
options.rationale: Gelatine is a protein; it is digested by a protease, not affected by starch.

options.content: Fresh pineapple's protease digests gelatine; heating denatures it in tins.
options.rationale: A denatured protease cannot digest the gelatine, so the jelly sets.

options.content: The protease in tinned pineapple was killed, but it comes back to life in the jelly.
options.rationale: Enzymes are not alive, and denaturation is permanent.

explanation: Gelatine is a protein, so the active protease in fresh pineapple digests it and the jelly cannot set. Canning heats the fruit enough to denature the protease: its active site changes shape permanently, so it can no longer digest the gelatine.
hints: Which enzyme digests proteins, and what does heat do to it?

stem:
Farai soaked small discs of filter paper in catalase solution and dropped one disc into hydrogen peroxide solution at each temperature. Oxygen bubbles formed on the disc and made it float up to the surface. He timed how long each disc took to reach the surface.

| Temperature / °C | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 | 60 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Time for disc to rise / s | 25.0 | 16.0 | 10.0 | 12.5 | 40.0 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the rate of reaction at 30 °C as $\dfrac{1}{\text{time}}$. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Between which two temperatures is the optimum most likely to lie?

options.content: 30 °C and 50 °C
options.rationale: The fastest rate measured was at 40 °C, and the rate was slower at both 30 °C and 50 °C.

options.content: 20 °C and 30 °C
options.rationale: The rate was still increasing above 30 °C.

options.content: 50 °C and 60 °C
options.rationale: The rate was already falling above 40 °C.

options.content: It must be exactly 40 °C.
options.rationale: Only 10 °C steps were tested, so the optimum could be anywhere between 30 °C and 50 °C.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: The disc took a long time to rise at both 20 °C and 60 °C. Explain why the reasons for the slow rate are different at these two temperatures.

points.description: At 20 °C: molecules have little kinetic energy, so there are few (effective) collisions / few enzyme-substrate complexes, but the enzyme is not denatured
At 60 °C: the catalase is (mostly) denatured; its active site has changed shape so hydrogen peroxide no longer fits

parts.explanation: At 20 °C the enzyme is active but the molecules move slowly, so effective collisions are infrequent. At 60 °C there is plenty of kinetic energy, but most of the catalase has been denatured: its active site has changed shape, so few enzyme-substrate complexes can form.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest **one** way Farai could make his results more reliable.

points.description: Repeat each temperature (at least three times) and calculate a mean, leaving out anomalous results

parts.explanation: Test at least three discs at each temperature and calculate the mean time, leaving out any anomalous result.

explanation: The rate at 30 °C is $\frac{1}{16.0} = 0.0625\ \text{s}^{-1}$. The shortest time (fastest rate) was at 40 °C, so the optimum lies between 30 °C and 50 °C. At 20 °C the enzyme is slow because molecules have little kinetic energy; at 60 °C it is slow because it is denatured.
workedSolution:
1. (a) Rate $= \frac{1}{16.0\ \text{s}} = 0.0625\ \text{s}^{-1}$ (3 significant figures).
2. (b) Fastest at 40 °C; slower at 30 °C and 50 °C, so the optimum is between 30 °C and 50 °C.
3. (c) 20 °C: few collisions, enzyme intact. 60 °C: enzyme denatured.
4. (d) Repeat and take a mean.
hints: A shorter time means a faster rate.
Is the enzyme damaged at 20 °C?

stem: A sample of an enzyme with an optimum pH of 7 was kept at pH 3 for 10 minutes. It was then moved to pH 7, but its activity stayed very low. What is the best explanation?

options.content: The acid denatured the enzyme, permanently changing the shape of its active site.
options.rationale: Extreme pH, like high temperature, can denature an enzyme permanently.

options.content: Enzymes always need several hours to recover fully from a change in pH before working.
options.rationale: A denatured enzyme does not recover, however long it is left.

options.content: The substrate was denatured by the acid.
options.rationale: The enzyme, not the substrate, was kept at pH 3.

options.content: pH 3 is the true optimum of this enzyme.
options.rationale: Its optimum is pH 7; it worked poorly at pH 7 only because it had been damaged.

explanation: pH 3 is far from this enzyme's optimum. The acid changed the shape of its active site so much that the enzyme was denatured. Denaturation is permanent, so returning it to pH 7 did not restore its activity.
hints: Is a change caused by extreme pH reversible?

stem: Tatenda is investigating the effect of temperature on the digestion of starch by amylase. Select **all** the variables he must keep the same in every test.

options.content: The temperature of the water bath
options.rationale: This is the independent variable he is changing.

options.content: The volume and concentration of the starch solution
options.rationale: More substrate would change the time taken.

options.content: The time taken for the starch to disappear
options.rationale: This is the dependent variable he measures.

options.content: The pH of the mixture
options.rationale: pH also affects enzyme activity, so it is controlled with a buffer.

options.content: The rate of reaction calculated from the time
options.rationale: The rate is calculated from his results, so it cannot be kept the same.

options.content: The volume and concentration of the amylase solution
options.rationale: More enzyme would change the time taken.

explanation: Temperature is the independent variable and the time (and so the rate) is the dependent variable. Everything else that affects the rate must be kept the same: the pH (using a buffer) and the volumes and concentrations of the starch and amylase solutions.
hints: Which variable is he changing, and which is he measuring?

stem: State the approximate optimum temperature of most enzymes in the human body.
explanation: Most human enzymes work fastest at about 37 °C, close to normal body temperature.
workedSolution: 1. Human body temperature is about 37 °C, and most human enzymes have optimum temperatures close to it.

stem: Pepsin is a protease with an optimum pH of about 2. It passes with food from the stomach into the small intestine, where alkaline bile and pancreatic juice have neutralised the stomach acid. What happens to the activity of pepsin there?

options.content: It increases, because all enzymes work best in neutral conditions.
options.rationale: Each enzyme has its own optimum; pepsin's is about pH 2.

options.content: It stays the same, because pH affects only the protein substrate.
options.rationale: pH affects the shape of the enzyme's active site.

options.content: It increases, because the small intestine is warmer than the stomach.
options.rationale: Both are at body temperature, and pH is the change that matters.

options.content: It falls sharply: at the higher pH its active site changes shape.
options.rationale: The small intestine is far from pepsin's optimum pH.

explanation: Pepsin is adapted to the acidic stomach. When the acid is neutralised in the small intestine, the pH is far from pepsin's optimum: the shape of its active site changes, protein no longer fits well, and its activity falls sharply. Proteases suited to that pH, such as trypsin, take over.
hints: Compare the pH of the small intestine with pepsin's optimum.
